Ngl I didn't expect the course will be this interesting. As a year 1, this is so far the best course I've had up till now.

I'll first talk about the down sides of this course. The first 8 lectures are easy as hell, but then after introducing you to the Gaussian Probability Density Function, everything changes. The lecture notes gets wodier, trying to explain entropy and central limit theorem within 3-4 slides which is nearly impossible to understand. Also the revision materials are very limited, you really have to lookup resources for youself, otherwise the review questions are definitely not enough for mid term and final.

The course content is a very brief introduction to every area of communication system and information theory. What I really like about this course is the questions are like "mini-games"  to me. They will teach you some basic methods to enhance the communication system, for example huffman coding and Dijkstra algorithm. And there will be questions for you just follow the rules of methods to get the answer. Like solving a sudoku or puzzle, once you get familiar with the solving patterns, it'll be so fun.

And since this course is teaching a topic relevant to our daily lives, you'll be amazed by how those genius contributed to the telecommunication system that we got so used to. Unlike math, those stuff are too abstract sometimes.

Speaking of that, there will be actual, practical use of what you've learned in math courses, that's also what makes this course so intriguing.

sections.content:
The course, titled "A System View of Communications: from Signals to Packets," is an exceptionally well-structured and comprehensive introduction to the fundamentals of modern communication systems. The title is not just a name; it is a promise that the course delivers on perfectly. It takes students on a logical, bottom-up journey, starting from the most basic unit of information—the bit—and methodically building up to a functional understanding of a point-to-point communication link, complete with noise analysis and error management.

The curriculum is intelligently divided into three main conceptual parts. The first part focuses on the "Signals" aspect, addressing how to represent binary information as physical, time-varying waveforms. It introduces the crucial concepts of continuous vs. discrete-time signals, sampling (T
s
​
), and the key parameter we control in the lab: Samples Per Bit (SPB). The course then models the communication channel as a Linear Time-Invariant (LTI) system, a cornerstone of signal processing. This theoretical framework, using tools like the unit step function u(n) and the channel's step response s(n), is used to explain real-world channel impairments like attenuation, delay, and the blurring of signal transitions. This section culminates in a deep dive into Intersymbol Interference (ISI), vividly visualized through the construction of eye diagrams, which clearly demonstrates the trade-off between a higher bit rate (lower SPB) and a higher Bit Error Rate (BER).

The second part of the course transitions from identifying problems to engineering solutions. Having established ISI as a major obstacle, the curriculum introduces the concept of channel equalization. By developing an equivalent recursive model for the channel, y(n)=a⋅y(n−1)+(1−a)⋅k⋅x(n), the course brilliantly demonstrates how one can mathematically "invert" the channel's effect to "open the eye" and improve signal integrity. After tackling ISI, the course addresses the second fundamental challenge in all communication systems: noise. This introduces students to the statistical nature of noise, using Probability Density Functions (PDFs) to model its behavior, with a specific focus on the ubiquitous Gaussian (or "normal") distribution.

The final part synthesizes these concepts into a complete "System View." It formalizes the analysis of errors using a probabilistic binary channel model and derives the formula for Bit Error Rate (BER) as BER=P

This provides the "Packets" part of the course title, showing how raw signals are structured for reliable transmission. sections.teaching:
The teaching in ELEC1200, led by Professor Shibo Chen with the support of Instructional Assistant Cupid Chow, is exemplary. The pedagogical approach is characterized by its clarity, logical progression, and a powerful synergy between theoretical lectures and hands-on laboratory work.

Professor Chen's lectures are meticulously structured. Each lecture begins with a recap of the previous one and clearly outlines the topics to be covered, which helps in framing the new material. The concepts are built incrementally, ensuring that students are never left behind. For instance, the idea of a waveform is first presented graphically , then represented as a list of values, and finally expressed mathematically as a sum of delayed unit step functions. This multi-faceted approach caters to different learning styles and reinforces understanding. Complex topics like LTI systems and superposition are not just stated as facts; they are illustrated with clear, step-by-step graphical examples showing how an output signal is constructed from the system's response to basic inputs. Similarly, the abstract concept of an eye diagram is demystified through a detailed, slide-by-slide construction, showing how overlapping signal segments reveal the impact of ISI. The lecture slides are a fantastic resource—visually rich with diagrams, graphs, and concise mathematical formulations that are easy to follow.

The tutorials and lab support, presumably managed by Cupid Chow and the TAs, are the critical bridge between theory and practice. The tutorial slides clearly detail the lab logistics, from group sign-ups on Canvas to the specific procedures for checkpoints and post-lab quizzes. This level of organization removes administrative friction and allows students to focus on the technical content. The introduction to MATLAB in Lab #1 is essential, providing the necessary software skills that are leveraged throughout the subsequent labs. The teaching team has designed the labs to be a direct application of lecture concepts. For example, Lab 5 explicitly requires students to study the effect of noise and measure the BER, comparing the results to the theoretical analysis performed in lectures. This direct link is what makes the learning so effective. Students don't just solve an equation for BER; they generate a noisy signal, see the bit errors, count them, and then relate their empirical findings back to the Q-function and SNR theory.
sections.grading: The grading structure for ELEC1200 is transparent, multifaceted, and generally fair, designed to assess a student's abilities across a spectrum of skills including practical application, consistent effort, and theoretical mastery. The overall assessment is composed of Labs (25%), Homework (10%), a Midterm Exam (25%), and a Final Exam (40%).
sections.workload:
The workload for ELEC1200 is substantial and demanding, but it is also exceptionally well-structured, predictable, and ultimately very rewarding. The course establishes a consistent weekly rhythm that, if followed diligently, makes the heavy load manageable. It is not a course where one can afford to fall behind.

A typical week's workload can be broken into several components. First, there are the lectures. Attending and absorbing the dense theoretical material presented requires focus. The concepts build on each other rapidly; for example, one cannot understand equalization without first mastering LTI systems and the recursive channel model. This necessitates reviewing the lecture notes after class to ensure a solid understanding, which constitutes a significant time commitment.

A total of 23 lectures are given during this semester. Regarding lecture content, you may refer to other recent reviews. Though the total number of lectures may differ, the overall content is still the same.

There are 7 labs in total. The first lab is not graded, so you may skip it if you're pretty familiar with programming (Although you don't need programming basics to finish all graded labs). However, you are recommended to attend the corresponding tutorials before going to your lab sessions. The tutorials help you understand what you need to add / correct regarding the given code (not giving direct answers, but basically not far from that), and concepts in case you're not clear on them.

Extra tip: The files used in the lab sessions are released days before the lab (usually on Fri or Sat, in the week before your lab), so you can download the files and kind of pre-lab using Matlab online. If you completely understand what the code is trying to do and know how to add / correct code, you can consider skipping the tutorials as well.

There are 5-minute open-book post-lab quizzes for each lab session, and the questions are related to the concepts used in the lab. The quiz doesn't allow backtracking, so be sure you selected the answer that you think is highly probable to be correct before moving on to the next question. You won't be allowed to go back once you move on. By the way, you can use simple calculators during the quizzes.

Each assignment is divided into several parts. There are sub-questions for each part, and you need to submit each part separately on Canvas. Usually, you need to edit the PDF given on Gradescope, so you'd better have a tablet and a PDF editor at hand. You may need to add pictures to the PDF in certain homework questions, which means that you need the "edit" function instead of making notes on it. sections.workload:
In total, there are 3 homeworks and 7 (nearly weekly) labs.

Homeworks are in general quite lengthy but enjoyable to do. Each homework contains 3-4 questions, and each question has multiple sub-questions which involve calculations, word explanations and graph plotting. You are allowed to submit homework in written form or Latex form, which is why I decided to do my homework on HackMD. Each homework takes me around a day or so, so doing the homework as soon as possible is definitely a good idea.

Lab checkpoints are basically free as the TAs will help you out if you encounter troubles, so everyone gets full mark. Post-lab quizzes, however, are EXTREMELY stressful. You have only 5 minutes to complete 4 short questions, which involve looking at graphs and doing some calculations. The quizzes require you to have a clear brain and much preparation (both physically and mentally) to get full mark, so be prepared to experience some sort of mental hell.

The means of both midterm and final exams are surprisingly low considering the difficulty of the papers, but don't think that you can get a free A range without a fight. A range is around 25%, but you have to get really good scores to fit into the top 25% as the course content is fairly easy. The exam questions this semester are really standard, some even easier than homework questions. Therefore, if you studied the lecture powerpoints thoroughly, and know how to do homework and the provided review questions clearly, you should PROBABLY be able to answer most questions correctly.

sections.grading:
Grading policy:

Lab [Total: 15%]:
    Lab check-off points [5%]
    Post-lab quiz [10%]
Online homework [10%]
Midterm [25%]
Project [20%]
Final [30%]

---
LABS

Lab check-points are easy. Just read the labs and do them, and you can get the check points without much problem.

The post-lab quizzes on the other hand are quite difficult and stressful. You need to really revise the content and pay attention in the tutorial to get a good score on them. They are all 5 minutes long with 5 MCQ or text entry questions.

There are 7 labs in total, 6 of which are graded. The first one is a trial lab you get you familiar with the procedures. You must attend at least 5 labs to pass.

Mean (check-off points): 21.67/24
Mean (post-lab quiz): 16.29/29

---
HOMEWORK

The homework is not too bad. Just read the lecture slides and you should be able to do them. But, don't do them the day they're due - many of my classmates ended up not finishing on time due to them leaving it till the last minute.

There are 3 homeworks in total, and combined, they are worth 120 marks. Depending on how well you understand the content, they can take between an hour and a few days to do.

Mean: 99.83/120

---
PROJECT

The project this semester was creating a transmitter and receiver to reliably transmit a sequence of bits over a fairly noisy channel while conserving as much power as possible. Due to it being an online semester, you do the project in Matlab and transmit over a virtual channel.

But, I think just the content from the course is not enough to get full marks. Accounting for variations in the given channel (everyone's channel has different noise), I think I had one of the lowest power usages of anyone I knew, but I still lost a point for the power consumption part. In fact, nobody in my session got full marks for power consumption.

In addition to writing the Matlab code, you have to write a report detailing any experiments you did and how you got the result that you did.

(Update: I asked about the grading for this part. They create a sub-optimal reference solution using a simple noise reduction technique and a greedy search. They then compare your solution to theirs, and only if your solution uses less power will you get full marks.)

The report is worth 8 marks, your code is worth 5, and the power consumption is worth 7. It is overall worth 20 marks.

Mean: 10.6/20 SD 4.5

---
EXAMS

The exams are like a combination of the post-lab quizzes and the homeworks. It starts with a few homework style short answer questions. Then, there are a bunch of multiple-choice/text entry questions, not unlike what you would find in the post-lab quiz.

The long questions are similar in difficulty to the homework, but of course there is a time limit.

The rest of the questions are similar to the post-lab quizzes. However you get 2 minutes per question compared to the 1 minute per question you get in the actual post-lab quizzes. So, you have more time to do them.

Overall, I think the exams are not too bad. They are fairly doable if you revise the content and practice. (They are open-book, open-calculator this semester).

Mean (midterm): 27/36 SD 6
Mean (final): 31.3/50 SD 9.4

---
OVERALL

The overall mean is 66.58.

This semester, one can get A+ with 93% and A- with 79% (exact boundaries unknown). So, it seems the A range is fairly wide.

This is essentially a crash course into the systems communications aspect of computer science.
The course is divided into 3 parts:
1. Channel Transmission: This part focuses on how bits are transmitted through a channel and how errors can be minimised using channel coding, framing, equalizing etc.
2. Sharing of channels: This part focuses on how a channel/frequency is shared among multiple communications using different types of modulation and filtering
3. Layers of Communications: This part explores different layers of communication (Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Application etc.) and popular protocols associated with each.

All these ideas are reinforced during labs where these principles are applied by coding a physical transmitter using MATLAB. The content is not too difficult as long as you pay attention in labs and tutorials

1. Examine a voice communication system to identify the practical context of key theoretical concepts in ECE.

sections.teaching: The professor is great and he takes initiative to meet you after class and often comes to the labs just to inquire about your course progress and actively asks for feedback on his teaching, and about the course. He has a great accent and I personally loved the way he taught in class. Even if you meet him outside the class, in the corridor, he would greet you if he remembers your face from the class. Even the TA, Cupid Chow, was pretty cheerful, and the notes that she prepared were pretty great. You will not mind going to classes for this reason. Apart from that, both, the lectures and tutorials are only 50 minutes long. Hence, it should not be a problem.

sections.workload: I personally believe that you should take this course only if it is compulsory for your major requirements. Do not take this course unnecessarily as the amount of workload for this course is pretty high, with regular submissions of assignments and prelabs. There is a bit of cramming work that is required towards the end of the course, so I would suggest you start studying a few days in advance.

sections.content: Basic wireless communication theory, signal processing and error correction in the first half of the course, and the second half covering internet protocols and data transfer methodologies. This course feels like the first step before taking ELEC2100.
sections.teaching: Both the professors have very fluent English and teach well, but the course easily gets boring when there is no interactivity between lecturer and students. More than a few times, the professor would ask simple questions in class but no student would bother answering even if they knew the answers, making it clearly frustrating for the professors and even less interesting for the class.
sections.grading: This course requires you to learn many new concepts and once you are able to get acquainted with them, it becomes easy to do well. This is clearly one of those courses where the more you study, the higher marks you will probably get. The problem is that if you're not one to study much, you will be left far behind.
sections.workload: Each week you need to complete 1-2 pages worth of pre-lab assignment that often includes MATLAB scripting and plotting graphs. Since most students can't afford to have it on their personal computers, you're forced to work at the barn or library. Labs are conducted in pairs but these are to be done separately. There are also post-lab interviews where the TAs ask you questions based on the lab tasks(which are often hard to understand). Apart from this there were also a couple of written assignments  that take a few hours to complete at the very least. I suggest having some friends also in the class and discuss material with each other often
